title.full: ASEAN Green Future Project Phase 2.1 & 2.2 Report, Decarbonizing the Philippine Power Sector

publisher.full: Sustainable Development Solutions Network and ClimateWorks Centre

description: Philippines-specific renewable energy pathway achieving near-zero power sector emissions by 2060.
pathwayDescription:
Normative all-renewable pathway for the Philippine power sector aiming at near-zero emissions by 2060. It shares MAP1’s ambitious policy package (accelerated fossil retirement, no new coal or gas beyond commitments, 50 GW offshore wind by 2050) but excludes nuclear. With GHG social costs priced into the optimisation, power emissions fall from 29.4 to 4.6 MtCO2e (2025–2050), while investment reaches about USD 1,033bn, roughly twice MAP1.

The ASEAN Green Future regional research project is run by the United Nations Sustainable Development Solutions Network, Climateworks Centre, and local researchers from leading universities. The project develops national policy analysis and near-zero pathways that are meant to provide policy recommendations and support policy makers.

coreDrivers.policies: MAP imposes accelerated fossil retirement, no new coal/gas beyond committed projects, higher offshore-wind deployment and RE-share targets. The pathway prohibits nuclear and targets an all-RE end capacity.
coreDrivers.emissionsTargets: Normative pathway designed for near-zero power-sector emissions by 2060, with no explicit annual cap. The all-RE system reaches it under the ambitious-policy constraints, with GHG social costs priced into the least-cost objective.
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: Least-cost optimization makes technology capital/O&M/fuel costs a core driver. MAP2 internalizes monetized GHG externalities in the objective, shifting dispatch/build away from coal.
coreDrivers.investmentChange: Total cumulative investment in the power sector reaches USD 1033bn by 2050, but no low carbon breakdown is provided. MAP1, with the same scenario ambition, forecast half the investment in the power sector.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: Electricity demand is driven by common macro assumptions. Population follows the UN World Population Prospects 2019 medium-fertility projection.
coreDrivers.otherDrivers: Environmental externality valuation is a distinctive scenario-design driver: EPA social costs for CO2/CH4/N2O are added to the optimization objective, changing generation and lowering emissions relative to the paired no-externality pathway.

dependencies.dependency_description: Critical (Explicit): The ambitious-policy package is a necessary design condition for the all-RE outcome which includes accelerated fossil retirement, no new coal/gas beyond commitments, RE-share floors and 50 GW offshore wind by 2050, with nuclear excluded.

High (Explicit): The all-RE pathway still requires accelerated retirement of privately owned coal/gas plants and large new RE/storage projects within a market where government cannot directly command investment.

Critical (Quantitative proxy): MAP2's all-RE build requires about US$2.214tn cumulative generation investment and 52.15 US¢/kWh generation cost in 2060, making financing/affordability the strongest economic bottleneck among the modeled pathways.

Critical (Quantitative proxy): MAP2's externality-inclusive all-RE route reaches 97.4% RE in 2050 but pushes generation cost to 35.71 US¢/kWh, making consumer affordability the clearest social-acceptance risk.

Critical (Quantitative proxy): MAP2 front-loads the all-RE build to 213.1 GW by 2040 and 329.2 GW by 2050, with large HPS/BESS/hydro additions and surplus generation, so grid/flexibility infrastructure must scale very rapidly.
High (Quantitative proxy): MAP2 internalizes externalities and front-loads the all-RE build (213.1 GW by 2040), intensifying dependence on rapid storage, hydro and variable-RE scaling.

High (Quantitative proxy): MAP2 front-loads the all-RE build and reaches very high wind/storage/hydro capacity. Onshore wind reaches about 94.4 GW in 2050, close to the reported national wind potential, making resource ceilings a major constraint.
The scenario include social costs of environmental damage caused by GHG emissions in its optimization model to diminish system costs.
